div.p: Spanning from the late Nineteenth Century to the early 1970s, Marianne Moore's life was embedded in the turbulent history of Modernity. Collected here are short articles that link Moore (her life and her poetry) to her context.
If you would like to submit an article to this page, or add commentary or a note to an existing piece, please email ccmiller@buffalo.edu.
div.head: Flaunting it with Marianne Moore
div.p: In 1952, Marianne Moore won the Bollingen Prize, The National Book Award, and the Pulitzer Prize and became something of a household name.On Moore’s fame, see Elizabeth Gregory, “Stamps, Money, Pop Culture, and Marianne Moore,” Discourse 17.1 (1994): 132. This 1969 airline commercial featuring Moore capitalizes on her fame and helps Braniff International’s sales to nearly double. The “When You Got It, Flaunt It” campaign was masterminded by legendary ad man George Lois who describes it as:

"a zany, outrageous campaign that featured a smorgasbord of the world’s oddest couples, exchanging the screwiest and most sophisticated chatter heard on television. Our juxtaposition of unlikely couples was unprecedented, creating the perception that when you flew Braniff International, you never knew who might be in the seat next to you."George Lois, $ellebrity (New York and London: Phaidon Press, 2003), n. p. [50].

Bringing together unexpected pairs of celebrities—Andy Warhol and Sonny Liston, Whitey Ford and Salvador Dalí—Lois juxtaposes Moore and the crime novelist Mickey Spillane, suggesting in Lois’ words, “a famous, but not great, writer, who dared even talking to such a great woman.”Personal correspondence with George Lois, March 6, 2019.

Moore’s appearance in this commercial is particularly noteworthy because during this late career moment her poetics sometimes approximate, or at least stand proximate to, advertising. For example, the final stanza of her 1958 poem “The Arctic Ox” contains the sentence: “If you fear that you are / reading an advertisement / you are.” In the commercial itself Spillane takes the campaign’s tagline —“when you got it, flaunt it”—as Moore’s own authorial creation telling her, “You know, you got a way with words.” This is one of the delights of the commercial as we giggle along with Moore.For an extended reading of the commercial, see Benjamin Kahan, Celibacies: American Modernism and Sexual Life (Durham: Duke University Press, 2013), 56-59.
div.head: Marianne Moore, Muhammad Ali, and Late Night Talk Radio
div.p: By Linda Leavell with Elizabeth GregoryElizabeth Gregory spoke with Miles Kreuger in June 2018, and asked him to clarify several issues in my original anecdote. She has added those clarifications here. She also consulted George Plimpton, Shadow Box, (New York: Putnam’s, 1977), 123-133. (June 2018)

After Holding On Upside Down was published in 2013, I received a phone call from Miles Kreuger, who runs the Institute of the American Musical in Los Angeles.Miles Kreuger does not use a computer. His contact information is: Institute of the American Musical, 121 N. Detroit St., Los Angeles, CA 90036, (323) 934-1221. He had seen my book in a bookstore and told me that he knew how Marianne Moore came to write the jacket notes for Muhammad Ali’s album, I Am the Greatest. He asked me if I had ever heard of “Long John” Nebel. I had not.

Nebel hosted a talk show on WOR radio in New York during the 1950s. At a time when executives did not think they would have any audience during the wee hours of the morning, Nebel’s show played from midnight to 5:30 a.m. and proved surprisingly popular. Topics included UFOs, voodoo, ghosts, and other unexplained phenomena. WOR’s strong signal reached more than half the national population, and listeners would telegraph comments and questions into the show.“Long John Nebel,” Wikipedia. This article cites a biography of Nebel: Donald Bain, Long John Nebel: Radio Talk King, Master Salesman, Magnificent Charlatan (New York: Macmillan, 1974).

In the 1960s Nebel moved the program to radio station WNBC. Kreuger served as a frequent guest on the show, which by this time included a diverse range of topics including politics, medicine, and theater.. In those days you could phone in telegrams through Western Union by dialing 0 for operator. A Marianne Moore frequently telegraphed questions to the show and Kreuger once asked on the air if she was “the” Marianne Moore, the poet. She telegraphed that she was.

A short time later, Kreuger suggested to friends at Columbia Records, where he had formerly worked, that Moore write the liner notes for Cassius Clay’s comedy album, I Am the Greatest. Columbia thought that would be excellent; Kreuger called her (having found her number in the phone book). She recognized him from the radio and agreed. The album was released in August 1963 with her notes on the sleeve. Six months later Clay won the national heavyweight championship, converted to Islam, and changed his name to Muhammad Ali.

I Am the Greatest was nominated for a Grammy in 1964 and is now regarded as a precursor to rap. Like virtually every other white American at the time, Moore did not recognize the African tradition out of which Ali’s rhymed taunts grew. And yet she lauds his poetic expertise, praising him as a “master of hyperbole” and “a master of concision” Ultimately, she calls him “a smiling pugilist.”

Moore and Ali first met face-to-face in 1967 at a party George Plimpton hosted at the nightclub Toots Shor. The two were photographed together composing a poem about his upcoming fight with Ernie Terrell.
